title: smell
medium: oil on canvas, lavender oil diffuser
notes:
Most of our senses receive input from the environment, then send signals to the thalamus (a small relay station in the brain). Smell works differently.

Odor molecules bind to receptors in the nose that bypass the thalamus and connect directly to the hippocampus & amygdala (regions involved with memory, emotional regulation, & fear) extremely quickly, even by neuronal standards. That’s why a scent can change your state faster than a sound or an image can.

In controlled studies, lavender inhalation before bed has been found to lower the subject’s heart rate & self-reported anxiety, and it even increases deep, slow-wave sleep—without the subject making any conscious choice to relax.

References:
Goel, N., Kim, H., & Lao, R.P. (2005). An olfactory stimulus modifies nighttime sleep in young men and women. Chronobiology International.
Sowndhararajan, K. & Kim, S. (2016). Influence of fragrances on human psychophysiological activity: With special reference to human electroencephalographic response. Scientia Pharmaceutica.

title: taste
notes:
The feeling of “sleepiness” is the effect of adenosine, an organic molecule that builds up in the basal forebrain the longer you’re awake.

Contrary to popular belief, caffeine does not break down or remove this molecule. Instead, it blocks the receptors that adenosine would normally bind to—so the brain continues to build up adenosine, but does not register the signal. As caffeine metabolizes (or breaks down over time), adenosine can once again bind to its receptors, restoring your sleepiness.

Although individual metabolism varies, an average person should enter the sleep allowance zone roughly 8 hours after a 120-mg dose.

References:
Temple, J. et al. (2017). The safety of ingested caffeine: a comprehensive review. Front Psychiatry.
Landolt, H-P. et al. (1995). Caffeine intake (200 mg) in the morning affects human sleep and EEG power spectra at night. Brain Research.
Drake, C. et al. (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. J Clin Sleep Med.

title: sound
notes:
A recent study tested the effect of earplugs versus pink noise (a sound similar to steady rainfall, with more energy at low frequencies), which has long been a popular sleep aid.

In the study, volunteers slept for seven nights under controlled aircraft, traffic, and alarm noise, both with and without pink noise and earplugs. The results showed that earplugs recovered most of the deep sleep lost to environmental noise. Pink noise, meanwhile, reduced REM sleep (the sleep stage most linked to memory & emotional processing) by nearly 20 minutes each night.

One possibility is that the brain never fully stops registering constant sound, even sound designed to be calming. Blocking noise protects one’s sleep in a way that adding noise does not.

References:
Basner, M. et al. (2026). Efficacy of pink noise and earplugs for mitigating the effects of intermittent environmental noise exposure on sleep. Sleep.

title: touch
notes:
Sleep is usually triggered by a drop in core body temperature—that’s why it is best to keep our bedrooms cool at night. Yet, counterintuitively, a hot bath before bed has been shown to facilitate the drop in body temperature.

Warming the skin allows peripheral blood vessels to widen, bringing warm blood away from the body’s core to the extremities. Keeping warm blood around the hands and feet allows the body to release heat more efficiently, in a process similar to sweating. Thus, the core is able to cool faster than it would otherwise.

Studies have found that a bath, 1–2 hours before bed, for as little as 10 minutes, encourages the body to fall asleep faster.

References:
Kräuchi, K. et al. (1999). Warm feet promote the rapid onset of sleep. Nature.
Haghayegh, S. et al. (2019). Before-bedtime passive body heating by warm shower or bath to improve sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews.

title: sight
medium: oil on canvas, LED light installation
notes:
There are several specialized cell types that make up your retina (the light-sensing layer on the back inside of your eyeball). One cell type in particular, the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ipRGCs, contains a pigment called melanopsin.

Melanopsin responds specifically to light at wavelengths near 480nm. This is the blue of the morning sky, as well as the same blue emitted by LED displays on phones & computers.

Retinal cells send signals to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN—a brain region that produces sleep hormones to regulate the body’s circadian rhythm. When activated, the retinal cells signal to the SCN to delay the release of melatonin (the primary molecule associated with sleep onset).

Technology at night doesn’t just delay your bedtime. It also delays your body’s endogenous sleep signal.

References:
Provencio, I. et al. (2000). A novel human opsin in the inner retina. J Neurosci.
Chang, A-M. et al. (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. PNAS.
Optional additional ref: Cajochen, C. et al. (2011), Evening exposure to a light-emitting diodes (LED)-backlit computer screen affects circadian physiology and cognitive performance. J Appl Physiol.
